mdp.d: The formalization of RL as the tuple \( (\mathcal S, \mathcal A, P, r, \rho_0, \gamma) \): states, actions, transitions, reward, initial state and discount. In an LLM, state = prompt + prefix, action = next token, transition = appending the token.

recompensa-esparsa.d: A reward that arrives at only a few steps of the episode. In LLM RL, usually only at the last token (EOS), with zero (or just the KL penalty) at every other one.

rollout.d: A trajectory generated by the policy: in an LLM, a response sampled for a prompt, together with the log-probs of each token. Generating rollouts is decode, which is why RL systems use inference engines such as vLLM or SGLang.

visao-bandit.d: Modeling the entire response as a single action, with \( \log\pi(y\mid x) = \sum_t \log\pi(y_t\mid s_t) \) and a single reward. It is the formulation used by RLOO and GRPO; the alternative is the per-token view of classic PPO.

retorno.d: The discounted sum of rewards from step \( t \) onward: \( G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k r_{t+k} \). With reward only at the end and \( \gamma = 1 \), it is practically the same for every token of the response.

atribuicao-de-credito.d: The problem of deciding which actions in an episode caused the reward. In LLMs, which of the hundreds of tokens earned the response its score. Baselines, the critic, TD and GAE are tools for this.

fator-de-desconto.d: A weight \( \gamma \in [0,1] \) that shrinks future rewards in the return. LLM RL almost always uses \( \gamma = 1 \); in GAE, \( \gamma < 1 \) works more as a variance reducer.

funcao-valor.d: \( V^\pi(s) = \mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid s_t = s] \): the expected return when following the policy from \( s \). In an LLM, “what score do I expect if I keep sampling from this prefix”.

funcao-q.d: \( Q^\pi(s,a) \): the expected return after taking action \( a \) in \( s \) and then following \( \pi \). In the token MDP, \( Q(s_t, y_t) = V(s_t \oplus y_t) \).

vantagem.d: \( A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s) \): how much better an action is than the policy's average in that state. It has zero mean under the policy itself; it is the weight of each token in the policy gradient.

critico.d: A network that estimates the value function \( V_\psi(s_t) \), trained by regression against a return target. In RLHF, an LM with a scalar head that emits one value per position, usually initialized from the reward model.

monte-carlo.d: Estimating an expectation by averaging samples: in RL, running complete episodes and using the observed returns. No bootstrap bias, but high variance.

truque-log-derivada.d:
The identity \( 
abla p = p\,
abla\log p \), which turns the gradient of an expectation into an expectation of gradients: \( 
abla\mathbb E_{p_	heta}[R] = \mathbb E_{p_	heta}[R\,
abla\log p_	heta] \). It makes it possible to optimize without differentiating through the sampling or the reward.

trajetoria.d: The sequence of states, actions and rewards of an episode, \( \tau = (s_0, a_0, r_0, s_1, \dots) \). In an LLM, the prompt and the response generated token by token.

policy-gradient.d: \( \nabla J = \mathbb E[\sum_t \Psi_t\,\nabla\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)] \), with \( \Psi_t \) = return, advantage, etc. In an LLM, it is the SFT gradient with each token weighted by its advantage.

reinforce.d: The Monte Carlo estimator of the policy gradient (Williams, 1992): \( \hat g = \frac1N\sum_i R(\tau_i)\sum_t \nabla\log\pi(a^i_t\mid s^i_t) \). Unbiased, but high-variance without a baseline.

estimador-nao-enviesado.d: An estimator whose mean, over many samples, is exactly the true quantity. It can still be very noisy: bias and variance are different problems.

baseline.d: A number subtracted from the reward in the policy gradient, \( (R - b)\nabla\log\pi \). If it does not depend on the action, it leaves the expected gradient unchanged and reduces the variance; the practical ideal is \( b \approx V(s) \).

rloo.d: A critic-free baseline: sample \( k \) responses per prompt, and each one's baseline is the mean of the other \( k-1 \). It equals \( \frac{k}{k-1}(R_i - \bar R) \) and is unbiased.

ator-critico.d: A family of methods with two networks: the actor (the policy, updated by policy gradient) and the critic (the value function, used as a baseline and to estimate advantages).

residuo-td.d: \( \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t) \): the “surprise” of a step, measured by the change in the critic's guess. If \( V \) is exact, its mean is the advantage.

retorno-n-passos.d: \( G^{(n)}_t = \sum_{k<n}\gamma^k r_{t+k} + \gamma^n V(s_{t+n}) \): it adds up \( n \) real rewards and fills in the rest with the critic. It is the advantage used by A3C (with \( n \le t_{\max} \)).

diferenca-temporal.d: A family of methods that learn a guess from the next guess (bootstrapping), such as \( V(s_t) \leftarrow V(s_t) + \alpha\,\delta_t \). Less variance than Monte Carlo, with bias when the critic is wrong.

lambda-retorno.d: The exponential average of the \( n \)-step returns: \( G^\lambda_t = (1-\lambda)\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda^{n-1}G^{(n)}_t \). \( \lambda = 0 \) is one-step TD; \( \lambda = 1 \) is Monte Carlo. It is the critic's target in GAE.

gae.d: The advantage estimator of Schulman et al. (2015): \( \hat A_t = \sum_l (\gamma\lambda)^l\delta_{t+l} \), computed back to front by \( \hat A_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda\hat A_{t+1} \). \( \lambda \) trades bias against variance.

decaimento-do-sinal.d: With reward only at the end, its direct contribution to \( \hat A_t \) falls off as \( \lambda^{T-t} \): \( 0.95^{500} \approx 7\times10^{-12} \). In long reasoning, the first tokens depend almost entirely on the critic; hence the decoupled λ (VC-PPO) and the adaptive λ (VAPO, SAO).

importance-sampling.d: Estimating an expectation under \( \pi \) with samples from \( \mu \), weighting each one by \( \pi(a)/\mu(a) \). Over a sequence, the product of the ratios explodes; that is why LLM RL uses per-token ratios, often truncated.

tis.d: Using \( \min(\rho, C) \) instead of the ratio \( \rho \): it trades a small bias for bounded variance (Ionides, 2008). Reintroduced for LLMs by Yao et al. (2025) to correct the vLLM × FSDP mismatch.

descompasso-treino-inferencia.d: The same weights give different probabilities in the inference engine (vLLM/SGLang, FP8/FP4 kernels, variable batch) and in the training engine (FSDP/Megatron, BF16). It turns on-policy RL into off-policy RL, and gets worse with quantization and MoE.

icepop.d: A training–inference mismatch correction used in GLM-5: it keeps a token's gradient only if the ratio \( \pi_{\text{train}}/\pi_{\text{inference}} \) lies in \( [1/\beta, \beta] \) (\( \beta = 2 \)), and zeroes out the rest.

kernels-batch-invariantes.d: Kernels (RMSNorm, matmul, attention) whose reduction order does not change with the batch size, so the same prompt yields exactly the same numbers. The foundation of “True On-Policy RL”; in vLLM, turned on by VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT. Same idea as batch invariance (ch. 4, 9 and 48).

routing-replay.d: Recording which experts the inference engine chose for each token of an MoE and enforcing the same routing in training. It tackles the largest source of mismatch in MoE: without it, ~94% of tokens switch experts in some layer.

a3c.d: The method of Mnih et al. (2016): several actor-learners in threads of a multi-core CPU, each with its own environment, applying n-step advantage gradients (with an entropy bonus) asynchronously to shared parameters.

hogwild.d: A lock-free style of parallel optimization: several threads write gradients to the same parameters at the same time, accepting occasional collisions. Used by A3C.

bonus-de-entropia.d: A term \( \beta\nabla H(\pi) \) that rewards less deterministic policies, to avoid premature convergence. In A3C, \( \beta = 0.01 \) (here \( \beta \) is the entropy weight, in the paper's notation, not the KL coefficient); in RLHF, the KL penalty usually plays this role.

a2c.d: The synchronous version of A3C: it waits for all actors to finish their segments and performs one batched update. It was the optimizer Christiano et al. (2017) used on the Atari games, in the first RL from human preferences.

impala.d: The architecture of Espeholt et al. (2018): actors send trajectories (not gradients) to a central learner and keep generating with stale weights; the staleness is corrected by V-trace.

staleness.d: How many weight versions separate the policy that generated a rollout from the one being trained. Asynchronous RL systems cap it (e.g., staleness 4 in MiMo-V2.6) and correct it with truncated importance weights.

v-trace.d: IMPALA's off-policy value target: TD residuals weighted by ratios \( \pi/\mu \) truncated at \( \bar\rho \) and \( \bar c \). The grandparent of TIS and IcePop: truncated importance for data from stale actors.

trpo.d: The method of Schulman et al. (2015): it maximizes the surrogate objective subject to an average KL \( \le \delta \) (0.01 in the paper), using the natural gradient, conjugate gradient and line search. It motivated PPO.

regiao-de-confianca.d: A limit on the size of the optimization step, within which the local approximation of the objective can be trusted. In TRPO it is measured in KL between the old and the new policy; in PPO, it is approximated by clipping the ratio.

lema-diferenca-de-desempenho.d: Kakade and Langford (2002): \( \eta(\tilde\pi) = \eta(\pi) + \mathbb E_{\tau\sim\tilde\pi}[\sum_t\gamma^t A_\pi(s_t,a_t)] \). The gain of a new policy is the advantage, computed with the old one, accumulated over the new one's states.

hessiana.d: The matrix of second derivatives of a function with respect to the parameters, \( H_{ij} = \partial^2 f/\partial\theta_i\partial\theta_j \): it describes the curvature. At a minimum (zero gradient), \( f(\theta+\Delta) \approx f(\theta) + \tfrac12\Delta^\top H\Delta \); the Hessian of the KL between policies is the Fisher matrix.

matriz-de-fisher.d: The Hessian of the KL between policies around the current parameters, \( D_{KL} \approx \frac12\Delta^\top F\Delta \), which can also be written as the covariance of the score function: \( F = \mathbb E[\nabla\log\pi\,\nabla\log\pi^\top] \). It measures distance in behavior, not in parameters.

gradiente-natural.d: The direction \( F^{-1}g \): the gradient corrected by the Fisher geometry (Amari, 1998; Kakade, 2001). It is the direction that raises the objective the most per unit of KL.

gradiente-conjugado.d: An iterative method for solving \( Fs = g \) using only products \( v \mapsto Fv \), without forming or inverting \( F \). It converges in at most as many iterations as the dimension; TRPO uses only a few.

busca-em-linha.d: Shrinking the step (exponentially, in TRPO) until the real objective improves and the real constraint is satisfied. It guards against steps that the quadratic approximation underestimated.
